prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language body of prose, rooted in poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture of rare formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu alone, with Carson (B011) and Wright (B019) as alternatives. I tested the case again against the chair's questions instead of treating the unanimity of round 1 as support. On the common criteria it still holds. The voice is distinctive and rests on language and imagery, not topicality. Formal ambition is carried through very large structures, as publicly described for Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid. The imaginative project joining memory, the body, dream and cosmology recurs across volumes. Poetry is the documented starting point of the prose. The scope of credit is clean: one writer, one language. My citation is a whole-oeuvre wording that names the Romanian language, the project and poetry as the root of the prose. It avoids a regional or period label. It also does not claim that the poetry has been assessed as a co-equal body of work, because I cannot assess it. That is how I would reconcile the six round-1 wordings. The chair asks which parts of the corpus are strongest and weakest, and whether anyone has expert commentary on the Romanian original. I cannot answer from the supplied evidence. I know the large novels from public descriptions, and I have no independent basis for ranking individual volumes or for judging how the sentences survive translation. Two things changed in my reasoning. First, on Nobel's 'idealistic tendency' I said in round 1 that his metaphysical architecture engages it more directly. After reading Mattson, Sward and Palm, I withdraw that as a discriminating point. The wording has been read in many ways over the years, and I do not think it separates Cărtărescu from Carson or Wright. The preference therefore rests on the literary criteria alone. Second, Olsson's proposal to rest a Carson citation on her written lyric and essay work makes B011 a more serious alternative than my round-1 treatment gave it. It does not change my preference.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. Romanian rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning cannot be checked through translation, and I have not independently verified any text. The question of pattern versus overextension in the very long late novels also stays open. Palm, Sward and Olsson read the recurring images as evidence that length is structural. I find that plausible, but it is an inference from descriptions, not from close reading, and I would not present it as settled. If the late volumes repeat the earlier project instead of extending it, sustained quality across the oeuvre would be weaker than the best books suggest. Corpus coverage is also uneven: the poetry and early prose are thinly known in translation, so the whole-oeuvre claim rests mainly on the large novels. Against the alternatives, Carson's formal invention is arguably less exposed to translation loss in English, as Sward says, and Wright's novels are real formal achievements. My preference for Cărtărescu depends on the breadth of his evidence across a long oeuvre, and that breadth is itself only partly tested.

responses.point: Olsson now places Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He proposes resting any Carson citation on the written lyric and essay work, with visual form as support. He accepts that her classical frame may narrow her range, and that translations and book-objects pose a question of authorship and scope.
responses.response: That narrowing answers my main objection to Carson, which was that the book-objects and translations made the citation scope hard to define. It does not fully answer the criterion of sustained quality. The question the chair raised is what in the written lyric and essay corpus carries quality across the whole oeuvre, and I cannot answer it with confidence from public knowledge. I know Autobiography of Red and Nox well enough to credit their invention. I do not know the rest of the corpus well enough to say it is uniformly strong. So I keep Carson as my first alternative, and I would not oppose her if close readers of the written work showed that the quality is sustained. I also agree with your point that the 'idealistic tendency' question is open. I have dropped my round-1 suggestion that it favors Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Sward holds Cărtărescu first and suggests anchoring the citation in the prose, naming poetry cautiously as formative ground. She says the translation problem may be less severe for Carson's and Wright's work in English. She also says Palm's argument moved her toward treating Wright as a closer alternative.
responses.response: I agree with the citation approach and have adopted it. The wording names poetry as the root of the prose but does not claim it has been assessed independently, which fits the thin translation coverage we both acknowledge. Your point on translation exposure is fair and I accept it. It is a real comparative cost for my preferred candidate. But I do not think it is decisive, since Carson's strongest effects also depend on form and Wright's on invented idiom and oral elements that I may not read fully. On Wright I am in the same position as you, with the same alternative. Her large novels are distinctive, and the main open question is whether the number of major works supports the criterion of sustained quality.

responses.point: Palm holds Cărtărescu first and Wright third. She says the thinner Wright corpus makes the case less complete, not weaker in kind, and that a later round could revisit it. She puts the burden on the citation to name the project instead of requiring every volume to be equal.
responses.response: I agree that Wright's case is less complete, not weaker in kind, and that is why she is my second alternative and not set aside. I also accept your point about the burden on the citation. Naming the project avoids implying that every volume reaches the same level. But I would add that this makes the claim honest and does not answer the overextension question. If stretches of the late novels are weaker, the citation can say so by what it names, but the committee still has to decide whether the strongest sustained work is enough. I think it is, on the evidence I know, with the caveat that I have not read the corpus closely. On Wright, I would want to see how the later work develops before treating the volume question as resolved.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg holds Cărtărescu first with Murnane and Michon as alternatives. He says the evidence does not settle whether the late novels extend the early project or repeat it. He accepts that Murnane's narrowness is a feature of the method and not a flaw, but that its breadth of significance is uncertain.
responses.response: I agree that the extension-versus-repetition question is open, and that our shared uncertainty here is more honest than the reading of length as structural. I cannot offer new evidence on the later volumes. On Murnane, you asked in round 1 for a case that the method widens. I did not rank him in my own top eight and still cannot argue the case from what I know. I treat his method as serious and disciplined, but I cannot show that it develops across the corpus, which is the criterion at stake. If you can name specific late works where the range widens, that is where I could change my view of him. Michon has a similar limit for me: sentence-level exactness is clear, but the small corpus and the loss of French syntax in translation make the whole-oeuvre claim hard to build.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning survives in English, French or other translations. I have no expert commentary on the Romanian original and cannot confirm this independently.
Whether the late, very long novels extend the early project or partly repeat it. Reading the recurring images as structural is an inference from public descriptions, not a result of close reading.
The poetry and early prose are thinly covered in translation, so a whole-oeuvre citation is only partly tested and rests mainly on the large novels.
Whether the written lyric and essay corpus of Carson carries sustained quality across the oeuvre if book-objects and translations are set aside, and how a citation would settle authorship scope.
Whether Wright's number of major novels is enough for the sustained-quality criterion, and how well I can read Aboriginal English and oral-form elements.

My comparisons rest on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions, not independent verification. Whether a co-opted member votes in committee is undocumented, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the actual award decision belongs to the full Swedish Academy.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile, and I do not request recusal. For transparency, the profile records that I was elected to the Academy in 2020 alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg, that I work with chair Anders Olsson, that I became Permanent Secretary on 1 June 2026, and that my own work is literary non-fiction, including a biography of Alfred Nobel that deals with the dispute over his will. That last fact is context for how I read the will, not a candidate-specific connection, and I have said above that I do not use that reading to discriminate among candidates. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
